Here's how marketers should spend their time in an automated Google Ads world.

Data from 707 marketers.

Last month Google added a report to Search Console that most business owners have never opened.

Let me show you what it says. And what it leaves out.

Open Search Console, click performance, there's a new section, Generative AI.

It shows you impressions. That's how many times one of your pages appeared inside an AI answer. An AI Overview, or AI Mode.

And it shows which pages.

Think of it like a billboard company calling to tell you how many cars drove past.

Useful. Now here's what it doesn't tell you.

It doesn't show clicks. Because most of the time, there aren't any.

And it doesn't tell you whether the answer actually named you. Or whether it just read your page to write about someone else.

So what Google's handed you is half a map.

Google's AI. Impressions only.

The other half, ChatGPT, Gemini, whether your brand was named, how often, and against which competitors that's what Ubersuggest's AI Search Visibility shows you.

Follow to use these easy explainers to stay ahead of the competition!

Your content doesn't get quoted as a whole. It gets quoted in pieces. That's why listicles and roundups earned almost 22% of all citations in our survey of 1,000 marketers. Headers that say exactly what the section covers. Bullets where one bullet equals one fact. Tables for anything with numbers. If a piece can't stand on its own, it doesn't get quoted.

#AISearch #SEO #ContentStrategy #AIMarketing
Which Google Ads automation delivers the most value?

It's not a new ad campaign. It's the list of customers who haven't been back in six months. One message to all of them. Almost nobody sends it. That list is the cheapest revenue you'll ever find, and it's already sitting in your system.

#CustomerRetention #MarketingAutomation #SmallBusiness #NeilPatel

You can have the best answer on the internet and still get skipped. AI isn't reading every word. It's hunting for one clear line it can quote and move on. If you make that line hard to find, AI moves on to a source that didn't. Good content still matters. It just has to be easy to extract.

#AIMarketing #ContentStrategy #SEO #NeilPatel

Here's how companies look at ad automation by business size.

Both from an adoption and business impact perspective.

Not every marketing channel makes you money the same way. Paid ads and SMS are S tier. Email and GEO/SEO are A tier. Social media lands in C tier. Social is great for getting your brand out there. It just doesn't drive as much direct revenue as most people think. Need help putting these channels to work? Check us out at NP Digital.

#DigitalMarketing #MarketingStrategy #PaidAds #SMSMarketing #NPDigital

Eight years ago, I made a video on ranking #1 on Google. It's still my most viewed video ever, but ranking #1 doesn't mean what it used to. People aren't just Googling anymore. They're asking ChatGPT and other AI tools, and those tools only pick a few sources to quote.

In this video, I break down five specific things that get your website pulled into AI answers. That covers how AI engines actually read your content, why they favor human writing, how what people say about you off your site affects whether you get cited, and which questions send traffic back to you.

It's based on what my team has been seeing in our own research, including surveys of 1,000 marketers and an analysis of over 3,000 pieces of content across 100 companies. If your content isn't showing up in AI answers yet, this is where to start.

How far does your conversion tracking go?

Only 4% track LTV. And 20% get all the way to revenue.

The lower you can go within your funnel, the better you can fine-tune your campaigns.

Search traffic down? Look at what you're optimizing for. Broad terms tell you nothing about what someone actually wants. Long tail queries tell you everything. Product, budget, size, color. Head to AnswerThePublic, type in your keyword, and start creating content around what people are really asking.

#SEO #LongTailKeywords #GoogleSearch #AnswerThePublic

Two-word searches are fading. People ask full questions now, even on Google. And they don't want a list of homework. They want one answer. This shift was happening long before the latest AI models showed up. Clear, direct answers are what get pulled into AI responses.

#AIMarketing #SEO #GoogleSearch #ContentMarketing

New York is always buzzing during Climate Week and the United Nations General Assembly. I come each year for the same reason: to have serious conversations that lead to meaningful change. 

Weeks like this aren’t about one person, one organisation or one big speech. They’re about showing up, listening, sharing knowledge and working together to turn ideas into action.

There are no easy answers to the challenges our world faces but spending time with so many brilliant, determined and hopeful people reminds me that progress is possible.

We all want to leave the world in a better place for our children and grandchildren, and the best way to do that is together.

So touching to see @VirginAtlantic’s new plane paying tribute to my wonderful wife, Joan. 
 
Joan was part of the Virgin Atlantic story from the very beginning. From joining the inaugural flight in 1984, to coming up with the idea of donating loose change on-board for charity (which resulted in almost every airline in the world following suit and raising billions over the years). She was always there. 
 
Seeing the details of our family tartan, the heart-shaped necklace, and the rings she wore every day, brought back so many happy memories.

Did you know that @Virgin once imagined the iPod, but we made it into an April Fool’s joke!

In 1986, we announced the Virgin Music Box: a machine that could store music and let you call up any song you wanted. We thought it was so farfetched it would pass as a ‘gotcha’ moment. How wrong we were!

Years later, the world caught up with the idea, and I remember thinking: we should have built the bloody thing. The moral of the story is that when an idea feels slightly ridiculous, don’t dismiss it too quickly.

Sometimes the ridiculous ideas are a not-so-distant future...

We give ourselves health checks. Our planet deserves one too.

Today, while in New York for Climate Week, I joined the Planetary Guardians and the brilliant Professor Johan Rockström to launch the 2026 Planetary Health Check, an annual scientific assessment of the systems that keep our Earth healthy.

The news is confronting. Seven of the planet’s nine safety boundaries have now been crossed, and all seven are moving in the wrong direction.

This isn’t some distant problem happening to somebody else. We feel it through hotter days, rising food prices, polluted air, floods, fires and droughts. It affects all of us.

But it’s not all doom and gloom - there are real reasons for hope. Solar power is doubling roughly every three years. One in four new cars sold worldwide is electric. And investment in clean energy is now nearly twice that going into fossil fuels.

The solutions are here. Now we need to use them at speed and scale to get our planet back into a safe space.

I want my grandchildren, and yours, to inherit a world every bit as beautiful as the one we’ve been lucky enough to enjoy.

Read the Planetary Health Check, share its findings and add your name to the call for planetary health to sit at the heart of global decision-making. This issue isn’t bigger than any of us, because every one of us can help.

When we see people attack empathy or say things like, “The fundamental weakness of Western civilization is empathy” (Elon Musk, 2025), we should ask ourselves, “What harm, pain, or hurt do they not want us to see or feel? Who do they want to hurt, humiliate, or dehumanize without accountability?”

Based on our research over the past 25 years, creating meaningful connections and human-centered systems requires a combination of compassion and cognitive empathy. I think of compassion as the daily practice and cognitive empathy as one its most powerful tools.

We define compassion as the daily practice of recognizing and accepting our shared humanity so that we treat ourselves and others with loving-kindness, and we take action in the face of suffering.

Most definitions of compassion share a commitment to action. It’s not just feeling, it’s doing. Compassion is fueled by accepting that we’re all made of strength and struggle—no one is immune to pain or suffering. Compassion is not a practice of “better than” or “I can fix you”—it’s a practice based in the beauty and pain of shared humanity.

Most researchers agree there are at least two elements to empathy: cognitive empathy and affective empathy. Cognitive empathy, sometimes called perspective taking, is the ability to recognize and understand another person’s emotions. Affective empathy, often called experience sharing, is one’s own emotional attunement with another person’s experience.

The empathy we desperately need is understanding what someone is feeling, not feeling it for them. If someone feels lonely, empathy doesn’t require us to feel lonely too, only to reach back into our own experience with loneliness so we can understand and connect. Affective empathy, feeling something along with the person who is struggling, is a slippery slope toward becoming too overwhelmed to offer meaningful support.

Again, empathy is a tool of compassion. We can respond empathically only if we are willing to be present to someone’s pain. If we’re not willing to do that, it’s not real empathy. And the lack of real empathy is 100% a major threat to civilizations.

@adamgrant and I loved talking with @angelalduckworth about her new book, “Situated.”

Big takeaway:

“To stay motivated through the countless hours of practice that separate amateurs from experts, grit is necessary but not sufficient. The situation also matters—and to an astonishing degree:

Culture matters.
Mentors matter.
Teammates matter.
Even the objects in your personal space matter.

How you think about your goals and what you’re willing to do to achieve them depends on both you and your situation.”

I also loved our conversation about billboards - those signs we post around our spaces as reminders of what’s important. It reminds of why I like to write in a room where my children’s art is hanging. The kids’ art is my favorite art and it’s imperfect and honest. Grit is great, but I also need the environment to say, “Have fun. Just start.”

Aaron Sandel @prof.sandel, an anthropologist and primatologist, has spent over a decade studying the Ngogo chimpanzees, witnessing one of the largest known chimp communities split into two factions.

Aaron also reflects on what it was like to watch chimps he knew by name turn against one another, while exploring the surprising depth of bonds in this community.

When it comes to addressing cheating in schools, in-class essays and oral exams can only go so far, writes @adamgrant, a contributing Opinion writer and organizational psychologist at the @whartonschool. “Creating obstacles is never going to be enough. We need to get at the root of the problem by changing students’ underlying motivations,” he writes.

“Across a series of studies, in a wide range of contexts, psychologists have found that as the stakes of a competitive challenge go up, cheating does, too,” he adds. “Some people are largely immune to this effect. They don’t follow a logic of consequence by calculating whether the benefits of cheating would outweigh the costs. They ask themselves: What’s the right thing for someone like me to do in a situation like this? They have strong moral identities.” 

Click the link in our bio to read about how schools can foster moral identities in students, from studying ethics to “inviting kids to think about how cheating is unfair to their friends.” | 🎨 @petey_royale #nytopinion

The people who help us grow are the ones who care enough to be honest with us.
